metadata.title: Teacher workload and intensifying demands: Lessons from the Chinese double reduction policy
metadata.venue: The International Education Journal: Comparative Perspectives

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a qualitative interview and focus-group design conducted in a public school in Zhejiang Province, Southern China, rather than an ILSA micro-data analysis. As such, there is no PISA/TIMSS-style sampling frame, plausible values (PV) generation, or complex survey weighting scheme to apply. The manuscript does not report any student-level sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis is based on thematic coding of interview transcripts. Therefore, weighting is not applicable to the reported findings; interpretation should focus on the reported stakeholder perspectives and policy-process implications rather than population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the study does not analyze cognitive achievement outcomes from an ILSA assessment (e.g., PISA reading/science/math PV-based scores). Instead, it uses semi-structured interviews and focus groups with teachers, administrators, principals, parents, and a student, and analyzes the data via thematic coding. Missing-data handling is not reported because the study does not describe a quantitative model-based estimation procedure that would require explicit missingness rules for PVs or covariates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Qualitative design: semi-structured interviews were conducted at one public school in Zhejiang Province, Southern China. The interview participants were one school principal, one administrator, and five teachers (each interviewed for about 45 minutes using the same set of questions). Parents and junior secondary students participated in focus groups and were recruited via advertisement on the school noticeboard and personal acquaintances/references (snowballing). The manuscript does not report any quantitative inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., assessment completion thresholds) because no ILSA micro-data sample was analyzed.

data.outcome_summary: This article is an empirical qualitative study examining teacher workload and related challenges under China’s Chinese Double Reduction Policy (DRP). It does not use PISA (or any other ILSA) micro-data, and it does not train or evaluate machine learning models. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with school leadership and teachers at a public school in Zhejiang Province, supplemented by focus groups with parents and junior secondary students. The findings are presented as thematic results: teachers report increased workload and longer working hours, inequitable or insufficient compensation, and tensions arising from mismatched expectations between parents and teachers. The study emphasizes school-level strategies (e.g., flexible teaching arrangements, temporary accommodation, parent-child cloud platforms) and argues for clearer remuneration guidelines and greater stakeholder collaboration. Because the design is qualitative, the results are not intended to estimate causal effects or population-wide achievement impacts.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction contains no ILSA program/cycle, no PV handling, no survey weights, and no ML techniques because the manuscript is a qualitative case study based on interviews and focus groups rather than an ILSA-based quantitative predictive modeling paper. Consequently, there are no student-level achievement targets, no PV-based outcomes, and no numeric model performance metrics to populate. The absence of countries and sample sizes per country reflects that the study is localized to one province/school case rather than an international large-scale assessment dataset.
